name: Hiring and Onboarding
title: Hiring and Onboarding
answer: AI can assist with hiring and onboarding tasks such as drafting job postings, organizing applications, scheduling interviews, and answering common new-staff questions, but the decisions about whom to interview and hire stay with people. The idea matters because automated screening can reproduce bias and create legal exposure, while human mentors and colleagues remain central to bringing new staff in well.

sections.body: This idea covers how AI fits into hiring and onboarding without taking over the judgment calls. AI can help write job postings and flag language that might put off qualified candidates, and it can help sort applications and arrange interviews. The problem it solves is administrative load, since hiring and onboarding generate a great deal of paperwork and repeated questions. At the same time, the text is clear that decisions about whom to interview and hire belong to people, not tools. The same split applies to onboarding, where an assistant can handle routine questions but people remain the heart of the process.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In a district office, AI might draft a job posting and check its wording, then help organize applications and schedule interviews while a hiring team reviews candidates itself. Any ranking or filtering tool is used only as a check rather than as the decision maker. For new staff, an onboarding assistant limited to district handbooks and policies can answer common questions at any hour, link to the official documents, and hand off to a person for anything it cannot answer. New teachers get special support in their first years, with mentors helping them use AI well, and AI helping mentors track goals and schedule check ins. Certification tracking in HR systems helps new teachers and the district keep up with licensing requirements. The text does not give separate grade band guidance for this idea.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text labels this idea with research on human review, citing Krugel et al., 2023, which found that when a machine ranks first, people tend to accept its choices. It also states that automated screening of candidates carries serious risks, because tools that rank or filter applicants can reproduce bias from past hiring patterns and expose districts to legal claims. The guidance that follows is that hiring teams should review candidates themselves and use any tool only as a check. No other study, figure or finding is given in the text.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The limits here are firm. Automated screening of candidates carries serious risks, and tools that rank or filter applicants can reproduce bias from past hiring patterns and expose districts to legal claims. Because people tend to accept a machine's ranking when it comes first, hiring teams must review candidates themselves and treat any tool only as a check. Decisions about whom to interview and hire stay with people. An onboarding assistant should be limited to district handbooks and policies, link to the official documents, and hand off to a person for anything it cannot answer, while human mentors and colleagues remain the heart of onboarding.
